questions.question: State the two conditions for a Platonic solid, and give the face shape, number of faces, vertices and edges of each of the five.
questions.expected_answer: Every face is the same regular polygon, and the same number of faces meets at every vertex (and the solid is convex). Tetrahedron: equilateral triangles, F 4, V 4, E 6. Cube: squares, F 6, V 8, E 12. Octahedron: equilateral triangles, F 8, V 6, E 12. Dodecahedron: regular pentagons, F 12, V 20, E 30. Icosahedron: equilateral triangles, F 20, V 12, E 30.

questions.question: Use the faces of the icosahedron to calculate its edges and vertices, explaining each division, and check your answers with Euler's formula.
questions.expected_answer: 20 triangular faces have 20 × 3 = 60 sides; each edge is shared by 2 faces, so E = 60/2 = 30. They have 60 corners; 5 faces meet at each vertex, so each vertex is counted 5 times and V = 60/5 = 12. Euler: V − E + F = 12 − 30 + 20 = 2, as required.

questions.question: Using interior angles, explain why there are exactly five Platonic solids.
questions.expected_answer: At least 3 faces must meet at a vertex, and their angles must total less than 360°, since exactly 360° lies flat and more cannot fit. Triangles (60°): 3, 4 or 5 at a vertex give 180°, 240°, 300°, the tetrahedron, octahedron and icosahedron; 6 give 360°, flat. Squares (90°): 3 give 270°, the cube; 4 give 360°, flat. Pentagons (108°): 3 give 324°, the dodecahedron; 4 give 432°, too much. Hexagons (120°): 3 give 360°, flat; larger polygons exceed 360° with 3. So exactly five combinations, and five solids, are possible.
